translation_history.english: From the Hebrews he (Postellus) tried to derive the origin of the Irish. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, plainly indicates the contrary—that "the land of Britain, before the coming of Christ," had by no means assented "to the religion of the one God"; indeed, Dio Cassius records by name that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others record that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons. And concerning their idol-madness Gildas, their own countryman, bears testimony so clear that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: "Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, shared with all peoples, by which the whole human race was held fast bound before the coming of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the very diabolical monstrosities of my homeland, almost surpassing in number those of Egypt, some of which, with their still-misshapen features, within or outside the deserted walls, we behold stiffening in their accustomed fashion with grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once destructive but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, etc."—so that concerning the most wretched condition of those times, and the most happy condition of those that followed, blessed Jerome did not hesitate to declare, in the epitaph of Nepotian: "Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the frozen region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean—peoples so innumerable, and the multitudes of so many nations? How varied in their tongues, in the fashion both of their dress and of their arms?"

For on the following page, Concordia, the wife of the apostle Peter, is reported to have been the daughter of Aristobulus and Salome. "St. Peter," says the author, "is held in honor in Spain, and his wife Concordia suffered at Rome under Nero, not long before he himself suffered. She was, as M. Maximus teaches in his commentaries on the epistle of St. Peter, the daughter of Aristobulus, or Zebedee, and of Salome; the mother-in-law also of Andrew, who married the other sister of Concordia, and of James and John. Now Aristobulus, surnamed Zebedee, was the brother of Barnabas, the apostle of the Lord." Thus far that author; and with him, concerning Peter's marrying the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of the apostle Barnabas, the Greeks also agree, in Metaphrastes in his commentary on Peter and Paul, and in the Menaia, at the 29th day of June.

latin_text: Ubi argutissimus criticus Scotici vocabulum, pro Scythici, reponendum esse conjicit: oblitus, apud Claudianum, Apollinarem Sidonium ac veteres illos, primam Scotici nominis syllabam semper productam legi; et in antiquis manuscriptis Scottos geminata litera passim exarari con suevisse. Neque sui dissimilis est, quum addit, Perso nium “probare in conversione Anglicana Claudiam non potuisse esse Anglam,” quasi quisquam eam Dempsteri insaniret insaniam, ut Claudiæ temporibus Angliam quæ reret in Britannia: aut id argumentatione sua conficere non conaretur Personius, B. Claudiam cujus Paulus meminit, non fuisse Britannam illam, cujus formæ decus Trajano imperante Martialis laudaverit; et consequenter, absque ullo fundamento vel Scotam constitui vel Anglam. Quan quam argumentum illud, quo potissimum ille nititur, a temporis ratione deductum, non multum urgeat. Neque enim si in undecimo quem citavimus epigrammatum libello occurrrunt aliqua sub tertio vel Nervæ vel Trajani consu latu conscripta carmina; sequetur, et reliqua omnia eodem tempore fuisse composita. Et licet sub Trajano mortem poeta obierit: senem tamen decessisse cogitandum est, et prius familiariter usum esse Silio Italico, secundi belli

translation_history.english: Here that most ingenious critic conjectures that the word Scotici ought to be substituted for Scythici — forgetting that in Claudian, Sidonius Apollinaris, and those ancient writers, the first syllable of the name Scotici is always read as long, and that in old manuscripts Scotti was commonly everywhere written with a doubled letter. Nor is he unlike himself when he adds that Persons "proves, in his treatise on the English conversion, that Claudia could not have been English" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness so far as to look for England in Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not striving to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the reign of Trajan, and that consequently she is set up, without any foundation, as either a Scot or an Englishwoman. And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from the reckoning of dates, carries little force; for even if in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited there occur some poems written under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, one must nevertheless suppose that he passed away an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer of the Second Punic War.
